chunks: Decoding register fields from hex. The question: Given a register map and the register value in hex, find the value of each register field.
When you read a register, the number often comes out as hex, such as 0xB5A3.
To decode it, you convert it to binary, line the bits up against the register's map, and read each field as its own number. A field is a group of bits that form one setting.
The method is mechanical, so the skill is doing it carefully every time.
Think of a date written as 20261111. You know the first four digits are the year, the next two the month, and the last two the day.
The digits are the same, but position tells you what each group means. A register works the same way.
The map says which bits form which field, and you cut the number at those boundaries.
Hex: base 16. Each hex digit stands for exactly 4 bits. Bit numbering: bit 0 is the rightmost bit. Counting goes up to the left.
Field [m:l] : the bits from m down to l, inclusive, so [7:4] is 4 bits wide.
Mask and shift: slide the field down to bit 0, then AND it with a run of 1 seconds as wide as the field (AND keeps a bit only where both numbers have a 1).
Reserved bits: ("What registers are"): bits with no defined meaning, to be left as the map says.
A 16-bit register reads 0xB5A3. In binary, each hex digit becomes 4 bits: 1011 0101 1010 0011. Say the map says bit 15 is EN, bits 14:12 are MODE and bits 11:8 are GAIN.
Bit 15 is 1, so the device is enabled. Bits 14:12 are 011, so MODE is 3. Bits 11:8 are 0101, so GAIN is 5.
In code, MODE is (reg 12) & 0x7 : 0xB5A3 shifted right by 12 is 0xB, and 0xB AND 0x7 is 3. That is the whole idea.
"I convert the hex to binary four bits per digit, number the bits from zero at the right, then read each field [msb:lsb] as a binary number, using shift and mask in code.
For 0xB5A3 that's 1011 0101 1010 0011, so a 16-bit map with EN at bit 15, MODE at 14:12 and so on gives EN 1, MODE 3, GAIN 5, RATE 10.
Then I check reserved bits, signed fields and byte order, and translate the codes into real meaning."
